title: Inversion of Control Pattern
oneLiner: Hands control of execution to a framework or container, which calls into your code at the right moments, instead of your code driving everything itself.

hero.name: The Conductor
hero.catchphrase: Don't call the framework. The framework calls you.
hero.power: Inverts who's driving — a container or framework manages the overall flow, calling into your code exactly when it's needed.
hero.weakness: Makes control flow harder to read top-to-bottom — you have to understand the container's lifecycle to know when, or even whether, your code actually runs.
hero.origin: The Conductor appeared after a team's web server hand-rolled its own socket listening, request parsing, and routing loop from scratch for every single project, reinventing the same orchestration every time.

story.problem: Every new project hand-rolls its own socket listening loop, HTTP parsing, and routing logic from scratch — reinventing the same low-level orchestration that has nothing to do with the actual business features.
story.solution: The Conductor introduces a web framework that owns the whole request lifecycle. Developers just register handlers; the framework calls into them at the right moment — 'don't call us, we'll call you'.
story.result: Nobody writes socket-handling code anymore. Teams just plug in route handlers, and the framework drives everything around them.

before: Application code drives its own low-level control flow
The same orchestration logic is reinvented on every project
Business logic is tangled with infrastructure plumbing
after: A framework/container drives the overall control flow
Application code only supplies the pieces the framework calls into
Business logic stays separate from infrastructure plumbing

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A new project's first week is spent hand-rolling socket listening and HTTP parsing from scratch, again.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're writing the same socket-handling and routing code we wrote on the LAST three projects. None of this is our actual product.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Conductor appears on a podium, baton raised, ready to lead the whole orchestra so nobody else has to.
panels.speaker: The Conductor
panels.dialogue: Stop driving your own control loop. Hand ME the podium — register your handlers, and I'll call into them exactly when needed.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: app.get('/orders', handler) registers a callback. The framework owns the request loop and calls the handler at the right moment.
panels.speaker: The Conductor
panels.dialogue: You write handler logic. I decide WHEN it runs — parsing the request, matching the route, then calling you. Don't call us, we'll call you.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The new project skips a full week of infrastructure plumbing and starts on actual features day one.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We started writing actual product features on day one. Zero time spent reinventing request handling this time.

useWhen: You're building on top of a framework/container that manages lifecycle, request handling, or dependency wiring for you.
You want to focus application code purely on business logic, letting infrastructure concerns be handled elsewhere.
The same orchestration logic would otherwise need to be reinvented across many projects.
avoidWhen: The application is simple enough that hand-rolled, linear control flow is easier to understand than a framework's inverted lifecycle.
Debugging an inverted control flow (where does my code actually get called from?) would cost more than the boilerplate it saves.
You need full, explicit control over exact execution order — IoC's callback-driven model can obscure that.
commonMistakes: Treating 'Inversion of Control' and 'Dependency Injection' as identical — DI is one common technique for achieving IoC, but IoC is the broader principle (which also covers callbacks, event handlers, and template methods).
Losing track of control flow in a heavily inverted system, making it hard to trace 'when does my code actually run?' just by reading it top-to-bottom.
Fighting the framework's IoC container instead of working with it, reintroducing manual control flow the framework was meant to replace.
Over-relying on framework magic without understanding the underlying lifecycle, making debugging framework-level issues much harder.
explanation.realWorldExample: Web frameworks (Express, Spring, Rails) calling your route handlers, game engines calling your `update()` method each frame, and UI frameworks calling your component's render function are all Inversion of Control — the framework, not your code, drives execution.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Is this the same thing as Dependency Injection?

conversation.speaker: The Conductor
conversation.message: Related, but broader. DI is ONE technique for achieving inversion — the container hands you your dependencies instead of you constructing them. I'm the bigger idea: the FRAMEWORK drives execution, calling your code, not the other way around.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the real cost of working under you?

conversation.speaker: The Conductor
conversation.message: Traceability. When a framework calls your code instead of your code calling straight through, understanding 'why did this run, and when' means understanding MY lifecycle, not just reading top-to-bottom.

codeBattle.scenario: Your team keeps hand-rolling the same request-parsing, routing, and lifecycle-management code on every new backend project, none of which is actually your product's differentiating logic.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Conductor lets a framework own the request lifecycle entirely, so your team only writes the business-logic handlers it calls into — no more reinvented plumbing per project.

quiz.question: What does Inversion of Control fundamentally change?
options: Who drives the overall control flow — a framework/container instead of your own application code
The number of classes in the application
quiz.answer: Who drives the overall control flow — a framework/container instead of your own application code
quiz.explanation: 'Don't call us, we'll call you' — that inversion of who's in charge is the defining idea.

quiz.question: How does Inversion of Control relate to Dependency Injection?
options: DI is one common technique for achieving IoC; IoC is the broader principle
IoC requires DI to be disabled
DI is a completely different pattern with no connection to IoC
quiz.answer: DI is one common technique for achieving IoC; IoC is the broader principle
quiz.explanation: IoC covers callbacks, event handlers, and template methods too — DI is just the most commonly cited example.

quiz.question: What's a real trade-off of building on heavily inverted control flow?
options: It can be harder to trace exactly when and why your code gets called, just from reading it top-to-bottom
It always makes the application slower
It removes the need for any framework at all
It requires every class to be a Singleton
quiz.answer: It can be harder to trace exactly when and why your code gets called, just from reading it top-to-bottom
quiz.explanation: Understanding an inverted system means understanding the container/framework's lifecycle, not just linear code.

quiz.question: What's a real-world example of Inversion of Control?
options: A web framework calling your route handler when a matching request arrives
A function calling another function directly and returning its result
quiz.answer: A web framework calling your route handler when a matching request arrives
quiz.explanation: The framework owns the request lifecycle and calls into your code — a textbook example of inverted control.
